docs.title: Addictive Grissini Breadsticks: A Crunchy Italian Classic
docs.summary: There’s something undeniably satisfying about the crisp snap of a well-made grissini. These slender Italian breadsticks are more than a pre-dinner nibble — they’re a masterclass in simplicity.
docs.body:
There’s something undeniably satisfying about the crisp snap of a well-made grissini. These slender Italian breadsticks are more than a pre-dinner nibble — they’re a masterclass in simplicity. Thin, golden, and addictively crunchy, grissini bring a rustic elegance to everything from charcuterie boards to your next Netflix snack break.
Whether you’re a seasoned bread baker or just starting out, these are easy to make and impossible to stop eating.

Ingredients

1 72 Hour Pizza Dough

handful of flour

handful of semolina flour

Optional: sesame seeds, poppy seeds, or chopped rosemary for topping

Instructions for Grissini
1. Preheat your oven
Position a rack in the middle of your oven and place your Baking Steel on top. Preheat the oven to 400°F (200°C) and let it heat for 45–60 minutes to ensure it’s fully charged with heat.

Want that extra crunch? We baked these right on our Original Baking Steel. It’s the tool that turns your oven into a breadstick-making machine.
2. Stretch the dough
Lightly dust a sheet of parchment paper with a mix of semolina and bread flour. Place your prepared dough on top.
Using both hands, gently stretch the dough side to side until it’s about 10 inches wide. Then stretch the top and bottom to make it roughly 8 inches tall, forming a rectangular shape.
Dust the top of the dough with a bit more of both flours.

3. Cut and shape
Using a bench scraper or sharp knife, slice the dough lengthwise into ¼-inch thick strips — about the width of a pencil and 10 inches long.
Gently stretch each strip just a bit and arrange them on the parchment so they aren’t touching — this prevents them from baking together.

4. Add toppings (optional)
Lightly brush the dough strips with olive oil. Sprinkle with sesame seeds, rosemary, or flake salt if desired. Press gently so the toppings stick.
5. Bake
Place the parchment onto a pizza peel, and use it to launch the dough strips directly onto your preheated Baking Steel.
Bake for 15 minutes, then check. Bake for 5 more minutes, or until browned and crisp to your liking.
For an extra crackly finish, turn off the oven, crack the door, and let them sit for another 5–10 minutes.
6. Remove and cool
Use your peel to remove the parchment from the oven. Transfer the grissini to a wire rack and let them cool completely before serving. They’ll crisp up even more as they cool.
🥖 How to Store Grissini

Room temp: Store in a paper bag for up to 3 days.

Freezer: Wrap in plastic wrap and freeze for up to 1 month. Reheat at 300°F for 5–7 minutes to revive the crunch.

Final Tip
These grissini are light, crisp, and wildly addictive. Perfect with a glass of wine, a bowl of soup, or just eaten one after another straight off the rack.
Tips for Next-Level Grissini

Consistency is key – Try to roll the sticks to the same thickness for even baking.

Let them cool in the oven – Turn off the oven, crack the door open, and let them dry out a bit more for extra crunch.

Make it yours – Add chili flakes, parmesan, or garlic powder for a twist.

These Reheat Beautifully
Grissini actually hold up well the next day — just pop them back onto a Baking Steel or in the oven at 300°F for 5 minutes to bring back the snap.
Grissini are simple, rustic, and totally addictive. They’re the kind of thing you make once… and then every weekend after.
🥖 Grissini That Just Keep Going
These grissini are light, crisp, and wildly addictive. Pair with wine, dunk in soup, or snack straight off the cooling rack — no wrong moves here.
🔥 Pro Tips

Keep ‘em even – Uniform width = perfect crunch.

Let ‘em dry – After baking, crack the oven door and let the sticks chill inside for 5–10 minutes. Game changer.

Customize – Add chili flakes, Parmesan, or garlic powder to make them your own.

♻️ Reheat Like a Pro
Grissini keep beautifully. Pop them back on your Baking Steel (or a baking sheet) at 300°F for 5 minutes to bring the snap back to life.

“This is the most exciting thing I’ve been a part of since I introduced the original Baking Steel to the world,” Lagsdin explains. “One of my most favorite things to do is witnessing the amazing results that people have achieved with the Baking Steel – and it’s only going to get even more exciting to see the amazing 16 Inch New York-style pizzas that everyone will be able to create with this new square Pro version of the steel!”

The Baking Steel Pro has gotten a series of upgrades, making it a revolutionary product that pizza lovers never knew they needed. Until now. 
While the original Baking Steel sported a 16-inch round baking steel shape, the Baking Steel Pro sports a 16 Inch Square Baking Steel shape. The New Baking Steel Pro is giving us over 20% more landing area for your 16" Pizza.   
The added diametrical inches are highly significant, as they allow everyone to create considerably bigger pizzas – in true New York-style, featuring those famously large and sexy slices.   
This has never been possible to do in your home, but with the Baking Steel Pro, every pizza enthusiast gets to create this legendary style of pizza at home, serve it up for family and friends, and watch them fold up the slice as if they were walking down the avenues of Manhattan.

docs.title: Making Burgers at Home Can Be a Grind
docs.summary: There is no question about it that grinding your burger meat at home makes far superior burgers than even the pre ground meat or pre-formed patties you may already buy from your favorite butcher.
docs.body:
There is no question about it that grinding your burger meat at home makes far superior burgers than even the pre ground meat or pre-formed patties you may already buy from your favorite butcher.
You can really make the burger taste like you want it to taste like. The freedom to grind the cuts of meat to make your burger really sing is something that more people should be doing. The Kitchen Aid attachment makes this even easier.
What I like about Grinding my own meat:

You can control the cut of beef in your burger
You can control the amount of fat in your grind (nobody like 93% lean beef, get over it, it's a burger, it's not supposed to be healthy)
You can control the size of your grind (some places grid way too small)
If you want, you can season your beef before your grind
You can control your destiny

I've learned a lot about burgers over my years, none more important than my time under Tony Maws of Craigie on Main and Kirkland Tap and Trotter. Voted multiple times as the Best Burger in Boston and covering the front page of Bon Appetit once, Tony knows a thing or two about burgers and really instilled in me how important grinding your own meat is.
Back at the Baking Steel Test Kitchen, we set out to make the best burger a Home Cook can make. Our choice for combination of beef cuts are Chuck, Short Rib and Brisket. Now you may be thinking "those are really tough cuts of meat and take hours to cook to become tender" and yes, you are slightly correct but we are morphing these cuts into something better. Grinding the meat, breaks down the structure a bit, pushing all of those muscles and fats through a small die breaks down a bit.
To make things easy, we did an even 1/3 split on the cuts of beef. We diced them up into about 1" cubes and put them in the freezer where our grinding attachments are already situated. One of the big things to properly grind any types of meat is making sure all the components and products themselves are thoroughly chilled. The grinder heats up so much with the force it needs that you don't want the meat heating up and smearing on you (so it doesn't look like that pink stuff McDonalds puts in their "burgers").
Back to grinding. We remove the pieces from the freezer, assemble and start to grind. You want the speed on about 6 out of 10. Slowly add your meat and fat into the grinder and watch before your eyes, your future dinner. Once finished, patty up your burgers for whatever your application is, 2 oz. for smash burgers, 7 oz for dinner burgers, or crumbled up for cheeseburger pizza! Needless to say, if you want the best of something, you usually have to do it yourself. Nothing different when it comes to burgers. While there are some fantastic burgers out there, there's nothing better than the one that you grind yourself, throw on your Baking Steel Griddle and smash in your face.

docs.title: Crispy Sheet Pan Fries at Home Using a Baking Steel
docs.summary: Read up on this recipe for the perfectly crispy fries without the need for a fryer!
docs.body:
Crispy Oven Fries Without a Fryer (The Science)
Last Updated: January 25, 2026

The secret to unbelievably crispy fries at home isn't a deep fryer, it's a slab of steel that turns your oven into a high-powered crisping machine. If your oven fries always turn out a little limp, it's because they're steaming in the oven's hot air. To get a truly crispy crust, you need intense, direct heat.
This is where the Baking Steel comes in. Think of it as a massive heat battery for your oven. By placing your regular sheet pan of fries directly on top of a preheated Baking Steel, you blast the bottom with powerful, conductive heat. This sears the outside instantly, creating a crunchy, golden-brown crust that hot air alone can't achieve.

How This Method Makes Fries Crispier
Using a sheet pan alone relies on convection (hot air), which often steams fries more than it crisps them. Placing that same sheet pan on a preheated Baking Steel changes the game entirely:

Direct Conductive Heat: The Steel transfers heat 20x more efficiently than a ceramic pizza stone, searing the outside of the fries for a perfect crust.

Eliminates Hot Spots: It provides incredibly even heat across the entire pan, ensuring every fry cooks uniformly.

Faster, Crispier Cooking: The intense energy from the Steel cooks fries faster, preventing them from becoming soggy or oil-logged.

🔥 Ready to Fry Without the Fryer?
The Baking Steel Original turns your oven into a crispy fry machine. Grab one and transform your sheet tray game forever.

📝 Crispy Oven Fries Recipe (No Fryer Needed)
Ingredients:

5–6 Russet or Kennebec potatoes, washed (not peeled)
3 oz vegetable or canola oil
Salt and pepper, to taste

Instructions:

Preheat your oven to 450°F with a Baking Steel on a rack. Let it heat for at least 30-45 minutes for maximum power.
Cut potatoes into thin fries, about ¼-inch thick. This is key—thinner fries get crispier. Do not soak them in water.
In a large bowl, toss the cut fries thoroughly in oil. Ensure every single fry is lightly coated.
Spread the fries in a single, even layer on a standard aluminum sheet tray. Do not overcrowd the pan.
Place the sheet tray directly on the hot Baking Steel. You should hear a sizzle!
Roast for 15 minutes, then carefully remove the tray, toss or flip the fries, and return to the oven for another 10–15 minutes, or until golden and crispy.
Remove from the oven, season generously with salt and pepper, and serve immediately with your favorite dipping sauce.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do you make fries crispy without a fryer?

The key to crispy fries without a fryer is high, direct heat. By placing an oiled sheet pan of fries directly onto a preheated Baking Steel in a 450°F oven, you create intense conductive heat that sears the outside of the fries, mimicking the effect of a deep fryer and preventing them from steaming.

Is it better to bake or air fry french fries?

While an air fryer is great for reheating frozen fries, baking on a Baking Steel produces crispier results for fresh-cut fries. The Steel's direct heat transfer is more powerful than the circulating hot air of an air fryer, leading to a better crust and fluffier interior, closer to a traditional deep-fried texture.

Why are my oven fries not crispy?

Oven fries often turn out soggy for three reasons: 1) The oven isn't hot enough, 2) The fries are overcrowded on the pan, causing them to steam, or 3) There isn't enough direct heat. Using a preheated Baking Steel solves the heat problem, and ensuring fries are in a single layer solves the steaming issue.

Should you soak potatoes in water before making oven fries?

While many traditional recipes call for soaking to remove excess starch, we don't recommend it for this oven-fry method. The surface starch actually helps the fries develop a golden, crispy exterior when they hit the intense heat of the Baking Steel.
